questions.prompt: For the RC low-pass filter (series R, output across C), which expression is \(H(j\omega)=V_{o}/V_{s}\) obtained with the voltage-divider formula?
questions.explanation:
Treat the capacitor as an impedance \(Z_{C}=1/(j\omega C)\) and use the divider (reader Eq. 2.32): \(H=Z_{C}/(Z_{C}+R)=1/(1+j\omega RC)\). Multiply numerator and denominator by \(j\omega C\).
• \(R/(R+Z_{C})\) is the output across R (a high-pass).
• \(1/(1+\omega RC)\) drops the j (it would be real, with no phase shift).
• \(1/(1-j\omega RC)\) has the wrong sign: it would be a phase lead for a low-pass.

questions.prompt: What is the first step to find \(H(j\omega)\) 'directly' for an AC circuit (no differential equations)?
options: Replace each capacitor by \(1/(j\omega C)\) and each inductor by \(j\omega L\), then solve as if the circuit were resistive (divider, \(KCL/KVL\), nodal analysis)
Write the circuit's differential equation and solve it with the initial conditions
Set \(\omega=0\) and replace capacitors by open circuits
Convert every signal to the time domain and find \(v(t)\) at \(t=0\)
questions.explanation:
The point of phasors is that the \(e^{j\omega t}\) factors cancel and differential equations become algebra: every element becomes an impedance, and all the resistive-circuit tools (voltage divider, Thévenin, nodal analysis) apply (reader Sec. 2.4.4).
• Solving a differential equation is the 'hard way'.
• Setting \(\omega=0\) gives only the DC gain, not \(H(j\omega)\).
• Time-domain evaluation at \(t=0\) does not give a frequency response.

questions.prompt: An RC high-pass filter (series capacitor, output across the resistor to ground) has \(H(j\omega)=j\omega RC/(1+j\omega RC)\). What is |H| at \(\omega=1/(RC)\)?
questions.explanation: At \(\omega=1/(RC)\), \(\omega RC=1\), so \(H=j/(1+j)\). \(|H|=1/\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}}=1/\sqrt{2}=0.7071\ (-3\ \mathrm{dB}\), the corner frequency). The phase is \(90^{\circ}-45^{\circ}=+45^{\circ}\).

questions.prompt: For the same circuit (\(R_{1}=1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) in series; \(R_{2}=1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\parallel C=100\ \mathrm{nF}\) to ground; \(\omega=10\ \mathrm{krad}/\mathrm{s}\)), what is the phase of \(V_{o}/V_{s}\) in degrees? (Give a negative number for a lag.)
questions.explanation:
\(H=(500-j500)/(1500-j500)\). Phase of numerator: −45°. Phase of denominator: \(-\tan^{-1}(500/1500)=-18.43^{\circ}\).
\(\angle H=-45^{\circ}-(-18.43^{\circ})=-26.57^{\circ}\).
Common mistake: subtracting in the wrong direction (−63.4°), or reporting only the numerator's phase (−45°).

questions.prompt: A series R–L–C circuit is driven by \(v_{s}\). The output \(v_{o}\) is taken across the capacitor. Which expression gives \(H(j\omega)=V_{o}/V_{s}\)?
questions.explanation:
Voltage divider: \(H=Z_{C}/(R+j\omega L+Z_{C})\) with \(Z_{C}=1/(j\omega C)\). Multiply top and bottom by \(j\omega C\): \(H=1/(j\omega RC+(j\omega)^{2}LC+1)=1/(1-\omega^{2}LC+j\omega RC)\).
• \((j\omega)^{2}=-\omega^{2}\), so the LC term is \(-\omega^{2}LC\), not \(+\omega^{2}LC\).
• \(j\omega RC/(\ldots)\) is the output across R (band-pass).
• The R term must keep its j (it is the reactive/phase part of the divider).

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter (R, C) drives a load resistor \(R_{L}\) connected in parallel with C. Which expression is \(H(j\omega)=V_{o}/V_{s}\)?
questions.explanation:
Use Thévenin at the capacitor: the Thévenin voltage is \(V_{s}\cdot R_{L}/(R+R_{L})\) and the Thévenin resistance is \(R\parallel R_{L}\). The capacitor then forms a low-pass with this source: \(H=[R_{L}/(R+R_{L})]/(1+j\omega(R\parallel R_{L})C)\).
Check the extremes: at \(DC\ H=R_{L}/(R+R_{L})<1\) (the load draws current through R), and the pole moves to \(1/((R\parallel R_{L})C)\), higher than \(1/(RC)\).
• '\(1/(1+j\omega RC)\)' ignores the load.
• Keeping the DC divider but the old pole mixes the two effects.
• Keeping the new pole but \(H(0)=1\) ignores the DC loss.

questions.prompt: A two-stage RC ladder has \(R_{1}=R_{2}=1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) in series and \(C_{1}=C_{2}=1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) to ground: \(v_{s}\to R_{1}\to\) node \(1\ (C_{1}\) to ground) \(\to R_{2}\to\) output (\(C_{2}\) to ground), with no load. At \(\omega=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\ (\omega RC=1)\), what is \(|V_{o}/V_{s}|\)?
questions.explanation:
Nodal analysis: for the ladder, \(H=1/[1+3j\omega RC+(j\omega RC)^{2}]\). At \(\omega RC=1\): \(H=1/(1+3j-1)=1/(3j)\), so \(|H|=1/3=0.3333\) (phase −90°).
Common mistake: multiplying two single-stage responses, \((0.7071)^{2}=0.5\). The second stage loads the first, so the stages do not simply multiply.

questions.prompt: A source \(v_{s}\) drives a parallel LC tank (inductor L in parallel with capacitor C) in series with a resistor R. The output \(v_{o}\) is the voltage across R to ground. What is \(|V_{o}/V_{s}|\) at the tank's resonant frequency \(\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{LC}\)?
options: 1, because the L and C cancel and the signal passes
0, because the parallel LC tank looks like an open circuit at \(\omega_{0}\)
0.5, because the tank and R divide equally
It depends on Q, but it is never exactly 0
questions.explanation:
\(H=R/(R+Z_{\mathrm{tank}})\) with \(Z_{\mathrm{tank}}=j\omega L/(1-\omega^{2}LC)\). At \(\omega_{0}\), \(1-\omega_{0}^{2}LC=0\) so \(Z_{\mathrm{tank}}\to\infty\) (equivalently the admittance \(j\omega C+1/(j\omega L)=0\)), so no current can flow: \(H=0\).
A SERIES LC resonance does the opposite (a short, so the signal passes). Parallel resonance blocks.
• '1' is the series LC behavior.
• '0.5' would need the tank impedance to equal R.
• For ideal L and C the null is exact for any Q.

questions.prompt: Preview of series RLC circuits. Using the result from this skill, the capacitor-output transfer function of a series RLC is \(H_{C}=1/(1-\omega^{2}LC+j\omega RC)\). For \(L=2\ \mathrm{mH}\), \(C=0.5\ \mu\mathrm{F}\), \(R=20\ \Omega\), a 2 V amplitude source operates at the resonant frequency \(\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{LC}\). What is the amplitude of the capacitor voltage? (A later skill shows this is '\(Q\times V_{s}\)'.)
questions.explanation:
\(\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{LC}=1/\sqrt{10^{-9}}=3.162e+04\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), so \(\omega_{0}^{2}LC=1\) and the real part of the denominator vanishes.
\(H_{C}=1/(j\omega_{0}RC)=1/j(31{,}623\times 20\times 0.5\times 10^{-6})=1/j0.3162\), so \(|H_{C}|=3.162\) (this is \(Q=(1/R)\sqrt{L/C}\)).
\(V_{C}=2\ \mathrm{V}\times 3.162=6.325\ \mathrm{V}\): the capacitor voltage is larger than the source voltage.
Common mistake: assuming \(|H|\le 1\) because the circuit is passive.

questions.prompt: Preview of series RLC circuits. The same direct method gives, for output across R, \(H_{R}=j\omega RC/(1-\omega^{2}LC+j\omega RC)=R/(R+j\omega L+1/(j\omega C))\). For \(R=50\ \Omega\), \(L=10\ \mathrm{mH}\), \(C=1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) at \(\omega=5000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) (half of the resonant frequency \(10{,}000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)), what is \(|H_{R}|\)?
questions.explanation:
\(\omega^{2}LC=(5000)^{2}(10^{-2})(10^{-6})=0.25.\omega RC=5000\times 50\times 10^{-6}=0.25\).
Denominator: \(1-0.25+j0.25=0.75+j0.25\), magnitude \(\sqrt{0.5625+0.0625}=0.7906\). Numerator magnitude: 0.25.
\(|H_{R}|=0.25/0.7906=0.3162\) (and the phase is +71.6°).
Below resonance the response is small; it peaks at 1 only at \(\omega_{0}\). Common mistake: dropping the imaginary part of the denominator \((0.25/0.75=0.333)\).

questions.prompt: Preview of series RLC circuits. For the series RLC with output across R, \(H(j\omega)=j\omega RC/(1-\omega^{2}LC+j\omega RC)\). Check its limits with the impedance picture (C open at DC, L open at very high frequency). What type of filter is this?
options: Low-pass: \(|H|=1\) at DC and → 0 at high frequency
High-pass: |H| → 0 at DC and → 1 at high frequency
questions.explanation:
Direct impedance reasoning: at \(\omega\to 0\), the capacitor is an open circuit, so no current flows and \(V_{R}=0\). At \(\omega\to\infty\), the inductor is an open circuit, so again \(V_{R}=0\). At \(\omega_{0}\) the L and C impedances cancel, leaving only R, so \(V_{R}=V_{s}\) and \(|H|=1\). This is a band-pass response.
The formula agrees: numerator ~ \(\omega\) at low \(\omega\ (\to 0)\), and for large \(\omega\) the denominator ~ \(\omega^{2}\ (\to 0)\); at \(\omega_{0}\) the denominator is \(j\omega_{0}RC=\) numerator.
